cells.tense: Right now the hands are steady — what you tend for the people around you gets tended, and the evidence is the thing itself.
cells.ask: Say one sentence to someone who shares it: this particular thing stays because it gets kept — then let their version sit without correcting it.
cells.core:
You're tending something that outlasts the moment — a way of doing things, a thing your people carry. Not hoarding it and not scattering it: keeping it alive at the pace it actually grows. There's a kitchen where the recipe gets used and a corner where the tools live, and neither is a museum. Tending the shared thing and tending your own life pull at each other, and the pull is real. You hold both without making anyone choose.

What comes next you do in the open. Say the one sentence about what you're keeping and why, and let the next person pick it up differently than you would. That passes forward a version with your care visible, and the care is the part that lasts longer than the thing itself.

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead there's a version where everyone finally gets it, and you're straining toward that instead of standing here.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you're protecting that nobody's asked you to protect, and for a week let it stand where it is, untouched.
cells.core:
A garden watered every hour drowns. Worked well, the shared thing grows at the speed it was going to grow, and the hands around it rest between seasons. Shape gets added only where shape is missing. A practice carries itself. There's a bench where people use what's been passed down without anyone standing over them to check it's done right.

Right now you're ahead of the season — adding shape, protecting meanings nothing has threatened, pushing something into a form it hasn't taken. The care is genuine. What it's costing is the thing care was for. What you carry already knows how to survive a little neglect, and the proof is that it's still here. Let one piece go unattended and watch whether it falls over. Whatever holds after that is what you were actually carrying, and the pattern will teach you more than the effort has.

cells.tense: Your hands haven't touched the shared thing in a while, and part of you is still at the threshold of when they did.
cells.ask: Pick one practice from your people's past — a dish, a phrase, a song — and finish this line on paper: if this lasts another ten years, it's because ___.
cells.core:
A table set for a meal nobody sits down to still gets cleared. Worked well, the shared thing gets picked up and used and passed on, and the hands that carry it are ordinary hands on an ordinary day. There's a shelf where the tools live and somebody reaches for them without ceremony. What's wanted isn't more wisdom. It's the reach.

Right now that motion has stopped. The shelf is still there, and what's missing isn't knowledge — it's the hand that knows what to pick up next. That hand comes back through what you already hope for, not through trying harder. Start with one thing you'd want around when you're gone. Name the first small thing that would keep it around, and you'll find the current was there the whole time.

cells.tense: You're already shaping what your people keep, in the sentences you repeat and the ones you let go, but it runs as if it didn't need anyone's hand.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you do that keeps a shared practice alive, and say it plainly once: this stays because it gets done.
cells.core:
A recipe written in someone's handwriting only stays a recipe because someone keeps cooking it. Worked well, you know which practices are yours to keep going and which ones you're just borrowing — and you say so, out loud, where the people around you can hear it. The keeping has a name and a hand and a day of the week.

Right now you're already keeping this alive — the way you say certain things, the small rituals you repeat without a flag, the stories you tell the same way twice. You call it just how things are. It's care, and it's been doing real work for a while. What's kept doesn't need a better name, just a hand that admits it's holding the handle. Pick one practice you keep going and say plainly that it's yours to keep. What you've been serving isn't bigger than your grip on it.

attempts.check: The hardest unsupported claim would be saying what was inherited from a specific person or what happened at a specific ceremony — the record says only 'shared meaning and tradition,' so the past-tense cell locates distance without naming ancestors, a breakup, or a loss. A reader might object that stewardship just means 'I'm good with money or my stuff' rather than with what gets passed between people, so each cell ties the tending to what a group carries forward. The asks survive being wrong: counting what was actually passed on, saying why a practice survived, adding one sentence to a family recipe — each teaches something even if the read misses, and none requires money or another person's cooperation. The sentence that would serve the writer more than the reader is any line about 'the culture as a living thing' — cut; better to say what is actually being tended, put down, or assumed to tend itself.
